name: Purlace – PFAS State Ban Tracker
author: Tico

sections.description:
Purlace comes with each covered US state’s sale bans on products with intentionally added PFAS, by product category, with the date each starts and the law it comes from. You set each product’s category; Purlace shows which states’ bans reach it and from when, keeps your suppliers’ certificates with their dates, and warns you when an order would ship it into a state where its category’s ban has started and nothing on your record covers it. If you choose, it also tells the shopper, or stops the checkout, for that state. Purlace keeps a record and shows each state’s dates as we read them from the law’s text on November 13, 2026. It is not legal advice and does not make your shop compliant. Laws change and our table may be wrong or late: check the linked law, or ask a lawyer.

PFAS are chemicals some makers add to products on purpose. Some states ban selling products in certain categories, such as cookware, cosmetics, clothing and children’s products, when PFAS were added to them, each from its own date.

How Purlace is different

Purlace comes with the rules. Each covered state’s PFAS sale bans are in the plugin by product category, each with its start date, whether it reaches products sold from that date or only products made from it, its status, and the law and section it comes from. You set a product’s category instead of typing states and dates, and each rule starts acting on its own date.

The State table: PFAS bans by state and product category

WooCommerce › Purlace › State table shows every covered state by product category on one page. Each line gives the day a rule starts, whether it reaches products sold from that day or only products made from it, and its status: in force, not started yet, ended, delayed, challenged in court or repealed. Press a line to read its law below the table: its title and section, a link to the state’s own page, what it covers in its own words, its exemptions and the day we read it. Tick “Only my categories” to see just the categories set on your products, or “Only what has started” to see only the rules that have started. On a phone each state is a card. The states the table does not cover are named under it.

Each product’s categories

Open a product and choose the Purlace tab in its Product data box. Tick each kind of product it is, such as cookware, cosmetics, clothing and accessories, children’s products, carpets and rugs or ski wax, each with a line on what the laws mean by it. A child’s rain jacket is both children’s products and clothing. When no kind fits, tick “None of these”, so your record shows you looked.

The products list shows each product’s categories in a Purlace column, with “not set” in grey for products nobody has looked at yet, and its bulk edit sets the categories of many products at once. To set a whole shop category in one go, open WooCommerce › Purlace › Overview, pick the shop category and the kinds to add, and see how many products would change before you press. Products keep the categories they already have.

Restrict products by state at checkout

WooCommerce › Purlace › Checkout rules sets what happens for each covered state, on the classic checkout and on the Checkout block alike. By default Purlace only warns you: the order goes through and is written in a log. For any state you can choose “Also tell the shopper”, which shows your message beside the product in the cart and at checkout, or “Stop the checkout for this state”, which refuses the order and shows your message. The message is your own, one text for every state, with {product}, {state}, {category} and {date} filled in, and each choice starts with words of its own: those for “Also tell the shopper” do not say the order cannot ship. A law that is in court or has been put off only warns you, unless you tick “Act on it anyway” for that state.

To restrict shipping by state, Purlace goes by where the order is going: the shipping state of a US address, the billing state when nothing ships, your shop’s own state when the order is collected in person. An address outside the US is never flagged. You choose how long the log is kept: 30 days, 90 days, 1 year or 2 years.

Supplier certificates, with their dates

Keep your suppliers in WooCommerce › Purlace › Suppliers: a name, a contact e-mail if you want one, and a note of your own. On a product’s Purlace tab, choose the supplier it comes from.

Keep their certificates in WooCommerce › Purlace › Certificates: the file (a PDF, a JPEG or a PNG, up to 10 MB), the supplier, the day it was issued, the day it runs out or “No expiry date”, what it says in your own words, and what it covers: the products you choose, every product from its supplier, or a shop category and the categories under it. A product’s Purlace tab lists the certificates that reach it and lets you attach one. On the day a certificate runs out, by your site’s clock, it turns grey and no longer counts; one that runs out within 30 days says so.

Purlace never reads what a certificate says and never judges it: it keeps the file and your own words. Files you upload go to your Media Library. Anyone who has a file’s link can open it.

A supplier you remove keeps its name on its certificates, marked “supplier removed”; its e-mail and note are forgotten.

Exemptions and stock made before a date

On a product’s Purlace tab, mark a state only when the words of its law leave that product out: “Exempt in Minnesota”, with a reason such as used goods, regulated by the FDA, a use the state has found currently unavoidable, or one you write yourself. Where a law reaches only products made from a date, such as Washington’s, tick that this stock was made before it, and add the last day it counts if you know it. Each mark goes on your record, for that state only.

The same tab lists the labels some states ask for on that product, such as Connecticut’s, each in its law’s own words. A “made before” tick or a certificate never takes a label off that list; an exemption in that state does.

Your record, as a CSV or a printout

WooCommerce › Purlace › Overview opens with one line: how many products have their categories set, how many need attention, and how many certificates run out within 30 days. “Needs attention” lists each product in a banned category where the ban has started or starts within 90 days and nothing on your record covers it, with the states, the dates and what you could do next. Below it is the whole record, which you can filter by state, category, supplier and status. Export it as a CSV file, or open the print view and print it from your browser.

Getting started

The first time you open WooCommerce › Purlace › Overview, a card takes you through the first steps: set your products’ categories, one shop category at a time with a count for each; see the states that matter for those categories; then add a supplier’s certificate or choose what happens at checkout. You can finish it or skip it, and bring it back with one button.

Where Purlace speaks to you

Only where you work. The products list marks a product that needs attention in amber and carries one notice you can close, Purlace’s own screens carry that notice too, and a product’s Purlace tab says what is missing. Once closed, it comes back only when more products need attention. Nothing shows on your Dashboard or on any other screen.

What Purlace does not do

It does not test products, read or judge what a certificate says, or decide whether a product contains PFAS or whether a state’s law reaches your shop. A state not in the table is not covered.

Where the data comes from

Each row of the table is read from the law’s own text, on the state’s own page, and listed here with its section, its link and the day it was read. The same list, with what each law covers, ships in the plugin’s data folder (data/SOURCES.md).

California’s sections are read from the state’s own bulk file of its codes (https://downloads.leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/pubinfo_2025.zip), because its code pages answer our reader with a browser challenge. New York’s are read through the state Senate’s own open legislation service (https://legislation.nysenate.gov/), for the same reason. Virginia’s code page gives no start day: it is read with the act that wrote it (2026 Acts of Assembly, chapter 910, https://lis.virginia.gov/bill-details/20261/HB122/text/CHAP0910, read from the PDF that page links) and § 1-214 of the Code (https://law.lis.virginia.gov/vacode/1-214/), which puts an act in force on the July 1 after its session when it names no later day.

Some rules are label rules, not bans: for outdoor apparel for severe wet conditions, the law asks for the disclosure “Made with PFAS chemicals.” (Maine and Rhode Island from January 1, 2029; Colorado and California from January 1, 2025 until January 1, 2028, when their bans start; Connecticut from January 1, 2026). Connecticut also asks for a label on twelve other kinds of product from July 1, 2026, and New Jersey on cookware from January 12, 2028. Connecticut’s labels have no end day: its 2028 ban stands beside them, so “Stock made before” spares the ban and never the label. Purlace shows a label rule as its own line and never stops a checkout on it. Maine bans that apparel from January 1, 2032 through its every-product rule. Colorado also bans installing artificial turf with intentionally added PFAS from January 1, 2026 (C.R.S. § 25-15-605): a ban on installing, not on selling, shown as a note under Colorado. California asks cookware makers to list chemicals from the state’s designated list on the label from January 1, 2024: a note under California, not a sale rule.

Not covered by this table: Alabama, Alaska, Arizona, Arkansas, Delaware, the District of Columbia, Florida, Georgia, Idaho, Indiana, Iowa, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Massachusetts, Michigan, Mississippi, Missouri, Montana, Nebraska, Nevada, New Hampshire, North Carolina, North Dakota, Ohio, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania, South Carolina, South Dakota, Tennessee, Texas, Utah, West Virginia, Wisconsin and Wyoming. Purlace has no rule for them, which says nothing either way about their laws. New Hampshire’s pages refused our reader.

Not read yet: Maine’s food packaging ban (32 M.R.S. § 1733(3-B) and a department rule), whose page refuses our reader, and Washington’s third finding on other kinds of food packaging.

External services

Purlace does not contact any outside service.

Privacy

Purlace keeps its records in your site’s own database and sends nothing anywhere. A supplier’s contact e-mail is kept only when you type one, for you to see; Purlace sends nothing to it. Certificate files go to your Media Library, where anyone who has a file’s link can open it. The checkout log holds the time, the state, the product numbers, what happened and the order number; nothing in it names the shopper. It is cut down daily to the time you choose: 30 days, 90 days, 1 year or 2 years.

Purlace adds a suggested text to WordPress’s Privacy Policy Guide and takes part in WordPress’s own export and erase of personal data. A supplier is found by its e-mail; erasing blanks its name and e-mail and leaves its certificates marked “supplier removed”. A shopper’s checkout log lines are found through their orders; erasing cuts the order number and leaves the state and the products. This is not legal advice.

Deleting Purlace removes everything it keeps, on every site of a network, unless you tick “Keep Purlace’s records if it is deleted” on its Settings tab. Your certificate files stay in the Media Library either way.
sections.faq:
Does Purlace make my shop compliant?

No. Purlace keeps a record and shows each state’s dates as we read them from the law’s text on November 13, 2026. It is not legal advice and does not make your shop compliant. Laws change and our table may be wrong or late: check the linked law, or ask a lawyer.

Which states and laws does it cover?

The states the table covers: California, Colorado, Connecticut, Hawaii, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Minnesota, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, Oregon, Rhode Island, Vermont, Virginia and Washington. Each law, its section, its link and the day we read it are listed under “Where the data comes from” below.

Every other state is not covered: Purlace has no rule for it.

Does a state’s ban reach my shop if I am in another state?

Purlace does not decide that. Each law says in its own words who it covers, and the State table shows those words with a link to the law. Purlace goes by where the order is going, and you choose what happens for each state. If you are not sure a law reaches you, ask a lawyer.

What does “made from” mean?

Most bans reach products sold in the state from their date. A few, such as Washington’s, reach only products made from their date. When your stock was made before that date, tick the box for it under that state on the product’s Purlace tab, and add the last day it counts if you know it. That ban then no longer counts for the product. A label rule still does.

Can I mark a product exempt?

Yes, one state at a time, on the product’s Purlace tab: “Exempt in Minnesota”, for example, with a reason such as used goods, regulated by the FDA, or one you write yourself. Mark it only when the words of that state’s law leave the product out. Each mark goes on your record.

Where are my certificate files, and who can open them?

In your Media Library, like any file you upload. Anyone who has a file’s link can open it. Purlace never reads what a file says, and deleting Purlace leaves the files where they are.

Does it work with the Checkout block?

Yes. The checkout rule works the same on the Checkout block and on the classic checkout. Your message shows under the product in both, and a checkout you chose to stop is stopped in both.

How often does the table change?

We change it in a new version of Purlace when a covered law’s date or status changes, or when we read a new state’s law. The State table shows the day we last checked the laws. Purlace never fetches the table from anywhere: it comes in the plugin.

How do I set the categories of many products at once?

In the products list, tick the products, choose Edit in the bulk actions and use “Set Purlace categories”: add categories, set exactly the ones you tick, or mark “None of these”. For every product in one of your shop categories, use “Set for a whole shop category” on WooCommerce › Purlace › Overview: it shows how many products would change first, and adds categories without taking any away.

Will Purlace stop an order?

Only if you choose “Stop the checkout for this state” on Checkout rules. Until you do, every order goes through and only you are warned.

Does Purlace send anything anywhere?

No. Everything stays in your own site’s database, and the table comes in the plugin itself.

What happens if WooCommerce is switched off?

Purlace does nothing at all until WooCommerce is back, and says so in one line on the Plugins screen.

What happens when I delete Purlace?

Deleting it removes its own tables, settings and the marks it put on products, unless you tick “Keep Purlace’s records if it is deleted” on its Settings tab. Certificate files stay in your Media Library either way; your products, orders, theme and other plugins stay as they are.

Will Purlace put notices all over my admin screens?

No. Purlace shows one notice you can close, and only on the products list and its own screens. Your Dashboard and every other screen stay as they are.

California’s sections are read from the state’s own bulk file of its codes (https://downloads.leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/pubinfo_2025.zip), because its code pages answer our reader with a browser challenge. New York’s are read through the state Senate’s own open legislation service (https://legislation.nysenate.gov/), for the same reason. Virginia’s code page gives no start day: it is read with the act that wrote it (2026 Acts of Assembly, chapter 910, https://lis.virginia.gov/bill-details/20261/HB122/text/CHAP0910, read from the PDF that page links) and § 1-214 of the Code (https://law.lis.virginia.gov/vacode/1-214/), which puts an act in force on the July 1 after its session when it names no later day.

Some rules are label rules, not bans: for outdoor apparel for severe wet conditions, the law asks for the disclosure “Made with PFAS chemicals.” (Maine and Rhode Island from January 1, 2029; Colorado and California from January 1, 2025 until January 1, 2028, when their bans start; Connecticut from January 1, 2026). Connecticut also asks for a label on twelve other kinds of product from July 1, 2026, and New Jersey on cookware from January 12, 2028. Connecticut’s labels have no end day: its 2028 ban stands beside them, so “Stock made before” spares the ban and never the label. Purlace shows a label rule as its own line and never stops a checkout on it. Maine bans that apparel from January 1, 2032 through its every-product rule. Colorado also bans installing artificial turf with intentionally added PFAS from January 1, 2026 (C.R.S. § 25-15-605): a ban on installing, not on selling, shown as a note under Colorado. California asks cookware makers to list chemicals from the state’s designated list on the label from January 1, 2024: a note under California, not a sale rule.

Purlace has no rule for them, which says nothing either way about their laws. New Hampshire’s pages refused our reader.

Not read yet: Maine’s food packaging ban (32 M.R.S. § 1733(3-B) and a department rule), whose page refuses our reader, and Washington’s third finding on other kinds of food packaging.

External services

Purlace does not contact any outside service.

Privacy

Purlace keeps its records in your site’s own database and sends nothing anywhere. A supplier’s contact e-mail is kept only when you type one, for you to see; Purlace sends nothing to it. Certificate files go to your Media Library, where anyone who has a file’s link can open it. The checkout log holds the time, the state, the product numbers, what happened and the order number; nothing in it names the shopper. It is cut down daily to the time you choose: 30 days, 90 days, 1 year or 2 years.

Purlace adds a suggested text to WordPress’s Privacy Policy Guide and takes part in WordPress’s own export and erase of personal data. A supplier is found by its e-mail; erasing blanks its name and e-mail and leaves its certificates marked “supplier removed”. A shopper’s checkout log lines are found through their orders; erasing cuts the order number and leaves the state and the products. This is not legal advice.

Deleting Purlace removes everything it keeps, on every site of a network, unless you tick “Keep Purlace’s records if it is deleted” on its Settings tab. Your certificate files stay in the Media Library either way.
